topic: Bayes' Theorem: The Geometry of Changing Your Mind
target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students with basic algebra knowledge.

outline.topic: Bayes' Theorem: The Geometry of Changing Your Mind
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students with basic algebra knowledge.

sections.title: The Core Concept: Updating Beliefs
sections.content: Introduce the idea that probability isn't just a fixed number, but a 'degree of belief' that should change when new evidence arrives. Define the transition from Prior Belief to Posterior Belief.
sections.example: A 'Cloud-Bot' robot predicts rain. Initially, it thinks there is a 20% chance of rain (Prior). Suddenly, it sees dark clouds (Evidence). How much should its belief increase?

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Probability Square
sections.content: Establish a geometric foundation. Visualize the total probability space as a 1x1 square with an area of 1. Any event is represented as a sub-area within this square.
sections.example: Draw a 1x1 square. If the 'Prior' probability of rain is 0.2, shade a vertical column representing 20% of the square's total area.

sections.title: The Prior and the Likelihood (The Slicing)
sections.content: Introduce the 'Likelihood'—the probability of the evidence occurring given the event. In the square, this is represented by a horizontal slice that intersects our prior area.
sections.example: Suppose the 'Cloud-Bot' sensor beeps 90% of the time when it actually rains (True Positive), but also 10% of the time when it's sunny (False Positive). We slice the 'Rain' column at 0.9 height and the 'No Rain' column at 0.1 height.

sections.title: The Geometry of Evidence (Filtering)
sections.content: When the evidence (the beep) happens, all areas of the square where the evidence *doesn't* happen become irrelevant. We 'throw away' the parts of the square that don't match the observation.
sections.example: The screen dims the areas where the sensor stayed silent. We are left with two small rectangles: The 'True Positive' area (Rain + Beep) and the 'False Positive' area (No Rain + Beep).

sections.title: Normalization: The New Universe
sections.content: Explain that because the remaining areas must now represent the 'new' total certainty (100%), we must rescale/zoom into these remaining slivers so their sum area equals 1 again.
sections.example: Visually 'stretch' the remaining 'Beep' rectangles vertically until they fill the 1x1 square again. The ratio of the 'Rain' sliver to the 'Total Beep' area is the new probability.

sections.title: The Formal Formula (The Mathematical Map)
sections.content: Map the geometric actions (Slicing and Rescaling) to the formal algebraic notation of Bayes' Theorem: P(A|B) = [P(B|A) * P(A)] / P(B).
sections.example: Show that P(A) is the width of our initial column, P(B|A) is the height of our slice, and P(B) is the total area remaining after the evidence filter.

sections.title: Summary and Intuition Check
sections.content: Recap that Bayes' Theorem is simply a way of calculating 'the area of the target event' divided by 'the total area of all events that could have caused the evidence.'
sections.example: Animate the Cloud-Bot updating its internal meter from 20% to approximately 69% based on the geometric ratio we just calculated.

storyboard.title: The Core Concept: Updating Beliefs
lecture_lines: Probability is your degree of belief in an event.
New evidence should change how you view the world.
This update is the heart of Bayes' Theorem.
animations: Display the text 'Probability: Your Degree of Belief' in #ADD8E6.
Create a meter showing a '20% Chance of Rain' (#32CD32).
Update the meter to 69% as dark clouds appear (#FF4500).

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Probability Square
lecture_lines: Imagine all possibilities fitting inside a unit square.
The square's total area represents absolute certainty.
Your initial belief is a portion of this space.
animations: Draw a white 1x1 square representing all possibilities (#FFFFFF).
Shade a blue vertical column for 20% 'Prior' probability (#0000FF).
Add a label 'P(Rain) = 0.2' inside the blue column (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: The Prior and the Likelihood (The Slicing)
lecture_lines: We start with the probability of rain.
This "Prior" is represented by a vertical column.
Next, we consider how often evidence occurs.
A horizontal slice represents the likelihood of a beep.
This creates specific regions for rain and no rain.
animations: Add a horizontal slice at 90% height for 'True Positives' (#FFD700).
Add a horizontal slice at 10% height for 'False Positives' (#FFD700).
Highlight the 'Rain and Beep' intersection area in green (#00FF00).
Highlight the 'No Rain and Beep' intersection in red (#FF0000).
Label the horizontal slices as 'Likelihood: P(Evidence | Event)' (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: The Geometry of Evidence (Filtering)
lecture_lines: Evidence has arrived: the sensor just beeped.
We discard all regions where no beep occurred.
Only the "Beep" rectangles remain in our view.
animations: Dim all parts of the square except highlighted intersections (#555555).
Remove the dimmed areas, leaving only green and red.
Move the green and red rectangles to the center.

storyboard.title: Normalization: The New Universe
lecture_lines: These remaining slivers don't fill the square.
But they now represent our entire reality.
We must rescale them to sum to one.
This vertical stretching creates our new probability space.
The larger sliver becomes our updated posterior belief.
animations: Place green and red rectangles side-by-side in a frame (#FFFFFF).
Stretch both rectangles vertically to fill the frame height.
Highlight that the green area now dominates the space (#00FF00).
Display text 'Normalization: Adjusting to the New Total' (#FFFFFF).
Show the new total area equals 1.0 (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: The Formal Formula (The Mathematical Map)
lecture_lines: Let's map these areas to the algebraic formula.
P(A) is the width of our initial belief.
P(B given A) is the height of our slice.
P(B) is the total area of the remaining rectangles.
Bayes' Theorem simply calculates the ratio of these areas.
animations: Display the Bayes' Theorem formula in the center (#FFFFFF).
Highlight P(A) and point to the initial blue width (#0000FF).
Highlight P(B|A) and point to the slice height (#FFD700).
Highlight P(B) as the sum of Green and Red (#FFFFFF).
Box the entire formula to emphasize the final calculation (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: Summary and Intuition Check
lecture_lines: Bayes' Theorem turns evidence into updated knowledge.
We filter the world through what we observe.
Now you can update your mind with geometric precision.
animations: Show the robot's meter jumping from 20% to 69% (#32CD32).
Display the calculation: '0.18 divided by 0.26 equals 0.69' (#FFFFFF).
Highlight the takeaway: 'Evidence updates belief through geometry' (#FFD700).
